content: Frigophobia is a specific phobia characterized by an intense and irrational fear of becoming too cold. Individuals suffering from this condition often wear excessively heavy clothing or wrap themselves in blankets, regardless of the actual temperature of their surroundings. This condition has been associated with other psychological disorders, such as hypochondriasis and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). A study conducted in 1975 among ethnic Chinese in Taiwan suggested that frigophobia may have cultural links to koro, a condition in which male sufferers believe their genitals are retracting into their body due to a perceived deficiency of male element (yang). In the case of frigophobia, male sufferers may associate coldness with an excess of female element (yin). Frigophobia is defined as a persistent, abnormal, and unwarranted fear of coldness. This fear persists even when the individual is consciously aware that there is no real danger and despite reassurances from others. The condition is also referred to as cheimaphobia or cheimatophobia. The development of frigophobia is not innate but rather acquired through past negative experiences. These experiences may have occurred during childhood, at school, in the workplace, or during social events. In some cases, individuals may not even recall the specific event that triggered the phobia. People at risk of developing frigophobia often exhibit certain characteristics, such as a general predisposition to fear and anxiety, a high-strung personality, or adrenal insufficiency. The symptoms of frigophobia can manifest in mental, emotional, and physical forms. Mental symptoms include obsessive thoughts about coldness, difficulty focusing on anything other than the fear, repetitive mental images of coldness, feelings of detachment or unreality, fear of losing mental control, and fear of fainting. Emotional symptoms include anticipatory anxiety, which involves persistent worry about future situations involving coldness; terror, characterized by an overwhelming fear of coldness; and an intense desire to flee from situations perceived as cold. Physical symptoms may include dizziness, shortness of breath, palpitations or a racing heart, chest discomfort, trembling, a choking sensation, sweating, nausea, lightheadedness, numbness or tingling sensations, and hot or cold flashes. Since the symptoms of frigophobia can vary widely among individuals, it is essential for those experiencing these symptoms to consult a medical professional for an accurate diagnosis and to determine whether their symptoms are indeed related to frigophobia. Treatment for frigophobia focuses on addressing the underlying psychological mechanisms and helping the individual regain control over their emotional responses. Patients are encouraged to understand that their fear is unfounded and to work on altering their emotional associations with coldness. Professional medical advice is crucial for determining the most appropriate treatment plan. However, this approach can sometimes reinforce negative associations and may not always be successful. Relaxation techniques, such as controlled breathing and visualization, can also be helpful. While medications may alleviate anxiety symptoms in the short term, there is no specific drug designed to treat frigophobia, and medications do not address the root cause of the condition. In Chinese culture, frigophobia is referred to as Wei Han Zheng (畏寒症) and is believed to result from an imbalance between yin (the female element) and yang (the male element). Traditional Chinese beliefs suggest that working women are particularly vulnerable to frigophobia due to factors such as stress, menopause, pregnancy, and anemia. During winter, these women may experience symptoms such as cold extremities and back pain. Dietary treatments aimed at rebalancing yin and yang are commonly recommended. These include consuming chicken soup, turnip juice mixed with ginger juice and honey, red tea with ginger juice and sugar, yeast-containing foods like bread, spices such as ginger and chili pepper, and diluted vinegar. Acupuncture is often used in conjunction with dietary changes to enhance the effectiveness of treatment. In Singapore, cultural beliefs about frigophobia are similar to those in China. A case study of a 45-year-old housewife with frigophobia highlighted the strong influence of cultural beliefs on the condition. Treatment in Singapore often involves a combination of low-dose anxiolytics and antidepressants, along with psychological interventions. It is important for healthcare providers to consider the patient’s cultural beliefs about the illness and to adopt a treatment approach that aligns with both the patient’s and the therapist’s perspectives.
